comparison: Perfect agreement on PDLIM2 repression mechanisms (C1-C13). Both evaluations find the TCGA analysis and experimental validation convincing, supporting dual mechanisms of genetic deletion and promoter methylation. Peer reviewers explicitly note data are 'convincing' and accept findings without critique.

Perfect agreement on haploinsufficiency findings (C14-C20, C157). Both evaluations accept the mouse model data showing spontaneous tumor development in heterozygous and homozygous PDLIM2-deficient mice. Peer reviewers implicitly support these findings by noting the study 'reinforces the critical roles of PDLIM2 in suppressing lung cancer.'

Strong agreement on nanoPDLIM2 efficacy (C26-C37). Both evaluations find the tumor burden reduction and mechanistic data convincing. Peer reviewers describe experiments as 'well executed' and data as 'convincing,' matching OpenEval's assessment of comprehensive mechanistic support.

Perfect agreement on safety profile (C38-C50, C146-C147). Both evaluations accept tumor-specific delivery and absence of toxicity. Peer reviewers note 'nanoPDLIM2 approach was shown to exhibit efficacy with low toxicity,' aligning with OpenEval's assessment of comprehensive safety data.

Strong agreement on chemotherapy synergy (C52-C62). Both evaluations find the combination data convincing, with mechanistic support through MDR1 suppression. Minor difference: OpenEval includes C51, C63 (rationale claims) while peer review focuses on C52-C62 (actual results).

Strong agreement on immunotherapy enhancement (C65-C73). Both evaluations accept increased TILs, MHC-I, and improved anti-PD-1 efficacy. Minor difference: OpenEval includes C67 (background knowledge) while peer review focuses on experimental results C65-C66, C68-C73.

Substantial agreement on triple combination efficacy (C99-C106, C144-C145, C159-C160). Both evaluations highlight the 60% complete remission rate as a major finding. Peer review groups these with dual therapy limitations (C92-C94) and complementary mechanisms (C95-C98), while OpenEval separates these into distinct results.

Agreement on differential PD-L1/MHC-I effects (C78-C82, C84). Both evaluations accept that nanoPDLIM2 fails to induce PD-L1 while chemotherapy does. Peer review groups these with genetic validation (C85-C87, C90-C91), while OpenEval separates genetic validation into R9.

Agreement on genetic validation using PDLIM2-deficient mice (C85-C87). Both evaluations accept that synergy is abolished in knockout mice, demonstrating PDLIM2's requirement. Peer review groups this with PD-L1 mechanism (R7), while OpenEval treats as separate loss-of-function evidence.

Agreement on complementary mechanisms (C88-C91, C95-C97, C139, C141). Both evaluations accept that nanoPDLIM2 induces MHC-I while chemotherapy induces PD-L1, providing rationale for triple therapy. Peer review groups with triple therapy results, while OpenEval separates mechanistic rationale.

Perfect agreement on advantages over epigenetic therapy (C150-C155). Both evaluations accept toxicity data and broader applicability of nanoPDLIM2. Peer reviewers implicitly acknowledge advantages by noting 'potential for clinical implementation.'

Agreement on established PDLIM2 mechanism (C128-C135). Both evaluations treat this as well-supported background from prior work. Peer review groups with tumor suppressor role (C122-C127, C136-C137, C158), while OpenEval separates into distinct background categories.

Agreement on prior PDLIM2 tumor suppressor work (C121-C127, C136-C137). Both evaluations accept these as established findings from previous studies. Peer review groups with molecular mechanism (C128-C135), while OpenEval separates prior work from mechanistic details.

Agreement that dual therapies are insufficient (C92-C94). Both evaluations accept these as important negative results establishing need for triple therapy. Peer review groups with triple therapy results, while OpenEval treats as separate supporting observation.
